Part I

The System

Turning a repository into something a machine can reason about without reading every line of it.

Motivation

AI agents answer structural questions by reading everything

Ask an agent "what imports the persistence layer?" and it greps, opens files, and reads source until it has enough context. That is slow, expensive, and it forgets everything the moment the session ends.

The information it needs — imports, exports, call relationships, change history — is structural. It does not require reading implementation bodies at all.

Measured head-to-head: a cold agent with no graph described 30 modules in 105s / 86,885 tokens. DeBob described 44 modules in 21s / 34,013 tokens.

1 min Lead with the concrete measurement, not the philosophy. If asked: the agent's prose was initially richer, which we treated as a defect to fix rather than a win to claim — see the engineering-findings slide.
Core principle

Send a graph slice, never the source

Repository→ Deterministic analysis→ SQLite graph→ Targeted slice→ LLM

Everything left of the LLM is reproducible with no credentials and no network. The model receives a ModuleContext — imports, re-exports, declarations, call graph, churn, and the doc comments the authors themselves wrote. It never receives implementation source.

Deterministic confidence 1.0

Files, symbols, imports, calls, git stats. Never guessed, always reproducible.

Semantic confidence < 1.0

Responsibility text and architectural layer. Quarantined in its own table, tagged with the provider and model that produced it.

1.5 min The separation of measured fact from model guess is the design idea worth defending. Re-running init without --semantic never overwrites an enrichment.

Architecture

The build pipeline

// deterministic — no credentials, fully reproducible
Scanner        ignore rules · size cap · extension allowlist
  → Analyzers    tree-sitter: TypeScript · JavaScript · Python
  → Git          simple-git: churn, authors, hot files
  → Builder      merge · deduplicate · layer inheritance
  → SQLite       .debob/context.db

// optional semantic layer
  → Query        buildModuleContext — assembles the slice
  → LLM          describeModule · explainDiff · answerQuestion
  → semantic_enrichments

Analyzers implement a common LanguageAnalyzer interface. Adding a language means implementing that interface and registering an extension — no engine changes.

TypeScript/JavaScript is the full-depth analyzer: imports, exports, functions, classes, interfaces, extends/implements. Python is shallow: imports and function/class nodes only.

1.5 min The plugin interface is the extensibility answer. Be honest that Python support is shallow.
Semantic layer

What the model is actually given

For each module, one call receives a structured slice and returns both fields at once:

File: src/graph/builder.ts
Layer (heuristic): business

Imports (4):   ./types.js · ../scanner/types.js · …
Declarations:  function buildGraph (line 88) — merges analyzer output…
Calls into:    inheritLayersFromFiles · dedupeNodes
Called by:     runInit
Git stats:     churn 6.0 · authors 2 · modified 2026-09-10

→ {"responsibility": "…", "layer": "business"}

Merging the two former calls into one describeModule halved prompt spend, because summarizeModule and classifyLayer had been sending byte-identical context twice.

1 min Show that the prompt contains no function bodies — only structure and author-written doc comments. That is the privacy and cost argument in one screen.
Engineering

Three providers, automatic fallback

watsonx→ on failure → OpenAI→ on failure → OpenRouter

Providers are tried in order; the first that answers wins. A provider whose credentials are absent is skipped rather than treated as an error, so a dead key degrades to the next provider instead of failing the run.

OpenAI and OpenRouter share one OpenAICompatibleProvider base — identical wire protocol, differing only in URL, key and model.

69

7.3×
fewer completion tokens
1 min — optional, cut if short on time Exactly one call per module is the designed behaviour and was never achieved until the message-role bug was fixed.
The measured claim

A graph slice costs a tenth of the source

29,887
prompt tokens sent measured
3,356
completion tokens
~321,018
est. tokens if source were sent
~10.7×
reduction

Prompt and completion counts are reported by the provider, not estimated locally. The source-size figure is an estimate: 1.22 MB scanned at roughly 4 characters per token.

We never claim the reduction is exact. Teal figures are measured; amber is derived. Every run prints its own number, and it moves between runs because completion length varies.

1.5 min If challenged on the ratio, concede immediately that the denominator is an estimate and the numerator is not. Distinguishing the two is the point.

Interface

Seven commands

CommandPurposeNeeds LLM

enrich is the no-API-key path: export each module's graph context, let the coding agent already in the repo write the answers, import them back.

1 min predict-risk is the bridge into Part II — the ML model ships as a CLI command, not a notebook.
Staying current

Incremental updates and agent discovery

Content-hash updates

Only files whose SHA-256 changed are re-analyzed; the graph is patched in place. A sample post-commit hook runs update in the background after every commit without blocking it.

Auto-discovery

init writes a delimited block into the repo's AGENTS.md, so any coding agent finds the graph automatically. The block is idempotent — it regenerates only its own marked region.

This is the actual point of the system: not that our tooling can query the graph, but that any agent with shell access can, without knowing anything about the internals.

45s
What measuring found

Eight defects, found only by measuring

A quality comparison against a cold agent exposed bugs that no test caught, because each produced plausible output:

  • Exports was wrong on every call. getFileExports read exports edges, which only exist for re-exports — a file with ten exported functions was described as "Exports (0)".
  • The call graph was computed and discarded. 160 calls edges never reached the prompt.
  • Duplicate implementation. buildModuleContext existed twice; only one was live and nothing imported the other.
  • Dotted filenames never resolved. ./fetch-poems.api made extname() return .api, producing phantom nodes — found only by testing a second repository.
  • Context sent twice per module — merged into one describeModule call.
  • Message roles were flattened into a single user turn, demoting every JSON instruction to ordinary text and causing ~23 wasted retries per run.
  • Provenance was read before any call, recording a model that had answered nothing.
  • Non-source files polluted the ML dataset — covered in Part II.
1.5 min — strong slide for "what did you learn" Theme: every one of these produced believable output, which is why measurement rather than testing caught them.
Part II

Machine Learning

Supervised learning over graph-derived features — five classifiers, two baselines, and one finding that reframed the experiment.

The problem

Which file should you review first?

On any real codebase a small minority of files absorb most of the defects. Reviewers have finite attention and usually allocate it by intuition.

The task: using only structural and historical facts already in the graph, rank files so the risky ones surface at the top of a short review list.

This is a ranking problem wearing classification clothes. Nobody reviews 43 files; they review the top 5. That drives the metric choice later.

1 min Real problem, real user, our own data. Flag immediately that the label is a proxy — detail follows.
Dataset

Our first dataset was quietly broken

The three highest-churn files in the repository were PROGRESS.md, README.md and package-lock.json. A churn-based label marked all three risky — so early models were partly learning to recognise changelogs and lockfiles.

CategoryFilesIn dataset?
source kept43TypeScript, JavaScript, Python
documentation21excluded
dependency metadata3excluded
config2excluded

Filtering to real source cut 69 rows to 43 — and improved every downstream metric. Fewer, cleaner rows beat more, dirtier ones.

1.5 min — do not rush Data cleaning presented as a finding, not housekeeping. Excellent answer to "what was the hardest part?"
Features and target

Six features, and a label we are honest about

Features

  • churn_score — commit-weighted change frequency
  • author_count — distinct contributors
  • import_fan_in — modules importing this one
  • import_fan_out — modules this one imports
  • lines_of_code — physical size
  • layer — architectural role (one-hot)

Label proxy

A source file is risky if either:

  • a commit matching fix|bug|hotfix|patch touched it, or
  • its churn is at or above the 75th percentile (threshold 3.0)

Say this early: this is not observed defect data — we never had a bug tracker. Every number measures agreement with a heuristic, and that heuristic uses one of our own features. That becomes the central finding.

Class balance: 25 stable, 18 risky (42% positive).

1.5 min — critical setup Declaring the churn overlap NOW is what turns the leakage slide into a finding instead of a gotcha.
Method

Five classifiers, one pipeline, stratified 5-fold CV

Pipeline

Numeric → StandardScaler. Categorical layer → OneHotEncoder. Fitted inside each fold, so no test-fold statistics leak into training.

Validation

Shuffled StratifiedKFold, 5 folds, seed 42. Results are mean ± standard deviation across folds; ranking metrics pooled out-of-fold.

Models compared

Logistic Regression · Decision Tree · Random Forest · Calibrated SVM (RBF) · DummyClassifier (majority-class floor) · raw churn heuristic (domain baseline)

Two baselines, not zero. Without a floor, an accuracy number means nothing on an imbalanced problem.

1.5 min Stress the scaler being inside the fold, and the two baselines. These separate a careful experiment from a sloppy one.

2.5 min — main results Point at the error bars deliberately: on 43 rows they reach ±0.25. Honest summary — SVM and Logistic Regression are not separated by this dataset. Do not crown a winner yet.
The central finding

We got a perfect score. That was the bug.

With churn_score included, two models classify every file in every fold correctly:

1.000 ± 0.000
Decision Tree F1 — churn included leaking
0.748 ± 0.161
Decision Tree F1 — churn removed

Churn is part of the label definition — the upper-quartile rule is churn. A model given churn is not predicting risk; it is reconstructing the answer key. The flawless score was the symptom.

Both experiments ship. The churn-inclusive model is saved as random_forest_with_churn_diagnostic.joblib, tagged diagnostic_only — loading it for real predictions prints a warning.

2.5 min — THE slide. Strongest speaker. Never let the examiner find the 1.000 first. Presented by you it reads as maturity; discovered by them it reads as not understanding overfitting. Same number, opposite grades.
Baselines

A one-line rule appears to beat us. It doesn't.

BaselineAccuracyF1ROC-AUCVerdict
Raw churn heuristic0.925 ± 0.1680.800 ± 0.4471.000leaky
DummyClassifier0.583 ± 0.0380.0000.500fair floor
Best operational model0.861 ± 0.0920.831 ± 0.1040.880honest

Thresholding churn scores 0.925 accuracy and a perfect ROC-AUC — higher than any learned model. That is not evidence that ML is unnecessary here.

The churn heuristic has partial access to the answer, exactly like the leaky models — it belongs in the diagnostic group. Its ± 0.447 standard deviation gives it away: near-perfect on some folds, poor on others.

The fair comparison is the DummyClassifier floor: 0.583 accuracy, zero recall. Against that, operational F1 of 0.73–0.83 is real signal from author count, fan-in, fan-out, size and layer — with churn removed entirely.

1.5 min Skip this and an examiner opening metrics.csv finds the churn baseline looking hidden. Own it and explain the disqualification.
Evaluation choice

Ranking beats accuracy — but precision@5 is fragile

ModelP@5Recall@5P@10Recall@10
Logistic Regression1.000.2780.900.500
Random Forest1.000.2780.800.444
Calibrated SVM0.800.2220.700.389
Decision Tree0.600.1670.800.444
DummyClassifier0.600.1670.400.222

The dummy classifier — zero recall, one class for everything — scores P@5 = 0.60 purely from tie ordering. Precision@5 is the right objective for a review-list product, but on 43 rows it is a five-item statistic and a poor discriminator.

1 min Defensive slide. Pre-empts "you picked the metric that flatters you" by naming the weakness first.
Error analysis

Where the operational model is wrong

With churn the matrix is perfectly diagonal — the leakage again. Without it, errors appear in both directions, which is what an honest model on 43 samples looks like.

45s — cut if short Useful if asked "what kind of mistakes does it make?". False negatives matter more here: a missed risky file never reaches review.
Interpretation

What drives the operational model

These are global importances combined with per-file threshold checks — not per-file causal explanations. The prediction output labels them "influential signals" for exactly this reason.

45s If asked about explainability, the honest answer is that SHAP would give per-file attributions and we did not implement it.
Limitations

What these numbers cannot tell you

  • 43 rows, 18 positive. Fold-to-fold standard deviations reach ±0.25. No result separates two models with confidence.
  • The label is a proxy. We measure agreement with a heuristic, not observed defects.
  • One snapshot in time. last_modified_at is collected but unused — every row comes from a single point in history, so this is not future-defect prediction.
  • One repository. No cross-repository test, so nothing here generalises.
  • Precision@5 is five data points. Correct objective, unreliable discriminator at this scale.
  • Results move with the graph. layer is a feature, so re-running enrichment changes the numbers. Every figure here is tied to one graph snapshot.

The fix we would build next: construct the graph at HEAD~N and label a file risky if a fix commit touched it in the window after that snapshot. That removes the circularity, restores churn as a legitimate feature, replaces stratified folds with temporal validation, and turns precision@5 into a claim about the future.

1 min — do not skip Stating limits before being asked is worth more than another result.
Conclusion

What we actually learned

System

A graph slice describes a module at roughly a tenth of the token cost of its source — measured, with the estimated half clearly marked.

Supervised

Structural features carry real signal: F1 0.73–0.83 against a 0.000-F1 floor. SVM and Logistic Regression are indistinguishable on 43 rows, and we say so.

The finding we are most confident about

A perfect cross-validation score is a symptom, not an achievement. Our 1.000 F1 came from a feature that helped define the label — and the ablation that exposed it is the most useful thing this project produced.

1 min, then Q&A Finish on the leakage lesson, not a metric. Anticipated: why F1 over accuracy (imbalance — dummy gets 0.583 with zero recall); why so few samples (one repo, source-only filtering, and we report variance rather than hiding it); why not deep learning (43 rows).

If asked whether you tried unsupervised: "We also ran K-Means, DBSCAN and Agglomerative clustering. K-Means separated risk well — one cluster 23 stable / 2 risky — but clusters did not reproduce architectural layers, which is why we kept layer as a supervised feature."
